messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds, Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Name Reminders: Hearing related names
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For years, Amir had lived inside his body—muscle, breath, and rhythm—and the stage had been his sanctuary. A 41-year-old dancer, married, with a quiet life in a Midwestern city, he had traveled home to visit his extended family in the Middle East when the war reached his village. He had been walking with his cousin down a dusty road, past a field recently turned for planting, when the first shell landed. The explosion was so close that the air itself seemed to tear. He remembered the smell of fresh soil and something acrid, metallic, and the way his cousin’s name—Youssef—had been shouted by someone running past. Amir had been knocked flat, his ears ringing, his mouth full of grit. He crawled behind a low wall and lay there for what felt like hours, certain that the next shell would find him. His cousin was killed three blocks away, but Amir did not learn that until the next day.

In the months after he returned to the United States, Amir tried to go back to work. He taught a contemporary dance class at a small studio downtown. But the first time a student’s foot slapped the wooden floor in a percussive sequence, his chest seized. The sound—sharp, sudden, rhythmic—was not a footstep. It was the thud of a mortar landing in soft earth. He left the room without a word, his hands shaking. He started wearing noise-canceling headphones during his commute, but that only made things worse: without the buffer of ambient sound, his own breathing seemed too loud, and the smell of rain on pavement—that wet, earthy scent—would send him into a cold sweat. He began to avoid certain streets, certain neighborhoods, certain parts of town where the soil was dark and exposed after a storm.

His wife, Leila, noticed he had stopped talking about his day. He had stopped talking about much of anything. When she asked what was wrong, he said, “I feel dead inside,” and the words came out flat, as if they belonged to someone else. He did not tell her that he believed she could see it—the whole thing, the fear, the dirt, the moment he thought he would die—just by looking at his face. He was certain that his skin had become transparent, that the horror of that afternoon was written on him like a scar. He began to avoid eye contact with her, with his students, with anyone. At the studio, he stopped demonstrating movements and only gave verbal corrections from the corner of the room. Attendance in his class dropped. The studio director asked if he was okay. He said he was fine. He was not fine.

He had lost something he could not name. It was not just his cousin, though that grief was real and raw. It was the sense that the world had been orderly, that people were basically good, that life made sense. Now he looked at strangers on the street and felt only a hollow wariness. He had lost his faith in people, in the idea that anyone could understand or help. Even Leila, who loved him, seemed like a stranger he could not reach. He stopped going to Friday dinners at her family’s house. He stopped answering calls from his own brother. The isolation grew quietly, like a weed he could not see until it had choked everything.

What finally brought Amir to seek help was a moment in the studio. A new student had the same name as his cousin—Youssef. When the student introduced himself, Amir felt the floor tilt. He excused himself, walked to the bathroom, and vomited. He could not say the name. He could not hear it. He began to scan the class roster before each session, looking for names that might undo him. The studio owner told him gently that he needed to take leave or find help. Amir chose help—not because he believed it would work, but because he was afraid of what would happen if he did nothing. He was afraid of losing his marriage, his career, his mind. He was afraid that the deadness inside him had become permanent. He wanted to feel something again, even if that something was pain. He was terrified that he might not be able to.
